claims.text: A tailored aging heat treatment can induce uniformly distributed, coherent nanoscale precipitates in a high-entropy alloy.
The induced precipitates will improve yield strength relative to the as-cast, homogenized single-phase state.
The induced precipitates will improve ductility relative to the as-cast, homogenized single-phase state.
The induced precipitates will increase Young's modulus relative to the as-cast, homogenized single-phase state.
The induced precipitates will improve fracture resistance relative to the as-cast, homogenized single-phase state.
Successful coherent-precipitate formation requires a suitable alloy composition and a specific temperature-time aging regime.
Prolonged aging or unsuitable temperatures may cause precipitate coarsening or formation of incoherent phases.
Coherent nanoscale precipitates interact with dislocations.
Uniformly distributed coherent nanoscale precipitates deflect crack propagation.
Coherent precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase yield strength.
A small precipitate size and uniform distribution can maintain or slightly improve ductility.
A small precipitate size and uniform distribution can maintain or slightly improve fracture resistance.
Local reinforcement of the matrix by precipitates can increase Young's modulus.
The aging treatment is expected to increase yield strength by approximately 10-20% relative to the baseline.
The treatment is expected to maintain or modestly improve ductility and fracture resistance.
The treatment is expected to produce a modest increase in Young's modulus.
Precipitate coarsening or loss of coherency may prevent the anticipated mechanical-property improvements.
The magnitude of the mechanical-property enhancement may vary with alloy system and processing window.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says ductility and fracture resistance will improve, whereas the predicted outcome allows these properties merely to be maintained.

The central hypothesis predicts improvement in all four properties, but the falsification rule can be passed when yield strength improves and only one of ductility, fracture resistance, or Young's modulus is maintained or improved.

The boundary makes the benefit conditional on successful precipitate formation, while the falsification rule treats failure to form the specified precipitates as falsification rather than as failure to implement the intervention.
